source: Ko and Myers (2004) Designing the Whyline
finding: Pre-design studies of Alice programmers showed that half of errors came from false assumptions made while debugging, and most questions asked were why-didn't questions.
numbers: 50% of errors due to false assumptions in debugging hypotheses; 68% of questions were why-didn't, rest why-did; 85% of questions were about a single object.
quote: Programmers only asked why didn't questions about code that plausibly might have executed.
limits: Alice is a small educational language; the observational studies are described only briefly in this paper (it cites the authors' earlier study).
agent_relevance: Failures are best framed as a why-didn't question about an expected event. Add a prompt for the expected-but-missing event, not only the wrong output.

source: Ko and Myers (2004) Designing the Whyline
finding: Whyline tool tested on identical debugging scenarios with and without the tool. Debugging time fell a lot.
numbers: Six matched scenarios. Repeated-measures ANOVA F(1,5)=12.64, p<.02. Mean speed-up factor 7.8. Without group N=4 (C1-C4), With group N=5 (E1-E5).
limits: Tiny N (9 total), CMU HCI masters students, prototype in Alice, compared only six scenarios that happened to match across groups. Not randomised assignment on the same tasks.
agent_relevance: Large effect from answering a causal why-question directly with runtime evidence, versus guessing and editing code. Supports O5 (go backwards from the failure) as a first move.

source: Ko and Myers (2004) Designing the Whyline
finding: Within the 90-minute session, Whyline users finished more tasks.
numbers: With: M=3.20, SD=.457 tasks; Without: M=2.25, SD=.500; t(7)=3.0, p<.02; 40% more tasks. Whyline was useful for 19 of 24 questions.
limits: Same tiny sample (4 vs 5). Usefulness rose across sessions as the design was fixed, so early sessions are confounded with prototype problems (0 of 3 useful for E1, 5 of 5 for E5).
agent_relevance: Numbers are an upper bound from a tuned prototype; do not expect 8x from an LLM scaffold.

source: Ko and Myers (2004) Designing the Whyline
finding: Why-didn't support was decisive for user acceptance. A participant dismissed the tool when it could not answer a why-didn't question.
numbers: E1 on being unable to ask why-didn't: 'this thing is useless'. E2 ignored the why-is menu because she wanted to ask about something that had already happened.
limits: Anecdotal; two participants.
agent_relevance: The agent must be able to ask about absent events (what should have run but did not), which output-only tools cannot show.

source: Ko and Myers (2008) Debugging reinvented / Whyline for Java
finding: Java Whyline pilot: mostly novices with the Whyline found a colour bug much faster than expert Java developers with Eclipse.
numbers: Whyline N=9: median 4 min (range 1-12). Control median 10 min (range 3-38), 18 self-described expert Java developers from a prior study. p<.05 Wilcoxon rank sums. Whyline group more than twice as fast.
limits: Single task, small sample, unfamiliar code; control came from a different earlier study (not concurrent; interruptions removed). Authors say generality is limited.
agent_relevance: Cross-study comparison, so treat the effect as suggestive. Still shows that asking the right why-question beat expertise plus text search.

source: Ko and Myers (2008) Debugging reinvented / Whyline for Java
finding: Experts used the tool worse than novices. Experts speculated about causes first and only then looked for a question to confirm their guess; novices simply asked 'why is the line blue?'.
numbers: Report from the pilot (Whyline N=9); novices outperformed experts in the pilot; unpublished expert study: Whyline users 'twice as successful in half the time' on two ArgoUML bug reports (preliminary).
quote: The novices tended to say aloud, 'Why is the line blue?' and then ask that question directly
limits: Qualitative observation. The ArgoUML result is preliminary and unpublished in this paper.
agent_relevance: Competing explanation: expertise can anchor on a hypothesis. A scaffold should make the agent ask the neutral why-question before generating a guess.

source: Ko and Myers (2008) Debugging reinvented / Whyline for Java
finding: Baseline: without the tool, developers lose time to wrong initial guesses and to text search for relevant code.
numbers: Initial guesses wrong almost 90% of the time (authors' earlier studies). Baseline painting-bug task: median 10 min (3-38); text search for 'color' gave 62 matches over 9 files. Crystal (related tool): 30% more tasks, 20% faster in lab.
limits: 90% figure is cited from earlier work, not re-measured here.
agent_relevance: Strong prior that the first hypothesis is usually wrong: spend effort on collecting evidence before committing to a cause.

source: Ko and Myers (2008) Debugging reinvented / Whyline for Java
finding: Question coverage check: of nine real bug reports sampled from five open-source Java apps, eight could be turned into a Whyline question.
numbers: 8 of 9 reports had a suitable question; the missed one was a feature request. Translation difficulty was in choosing the subject of the question; harder subject meant answer further from the cause.
limits: Authors say this is a best case and does not show people would find the question or understand the answer.
agent_relevance: Question formation is a bottleneck: the agent needs help picking the subject object/event of the why-question.

source: Ko, DeLine, Venolia (2007) Information needs in collocated software development teams
finding: Observed 17 developers at Microsoft for 90 minutes each. The most frequently unsatisfied needs were about causes of program state.
numbers: Top unmet needs: 'What code caused this program state?' 61% unsatisfied, max search 21 min; 'Why was the code implemented this way?' 44%, 21 min; 'In what situations does this failure occur?' 41%, 49 min; 'What code could have caused this behavior?' 36%, 17 min.
limits: Observational, one company, 90-minute windows. Percent is share of queries not satisfied.
agent_relevance: Tools rarely answer 'what caused this state' questions, which is exactly slicing. It is an unmet need even for professionals.

source: Ko, Aung, Myers, DeLine, Venolia (2006) An exploratory study of how developers seek, relate, and collect relevant information
finding: Developers spent a lot of time on navigation mechanics. Many followed dependencies that the IDE could not show.
numbers: 10 developers using Eclipse 2.1.2. Average 35% of time on navigation mechanics. Each developer navigated about 65 (SD 18) dependencies; 42% (SD 20) were indirect dependencies the IDE did not support (e.g. variable use to the method that computed it).
limits: N=10, Eclipse 2.1.2 (2006 tooling), counts from video coding with measurement error acknowledged.
agent_relevance: Indirect dependency following is the manual form of backward slicing. An agent with a slice tool saves the cost humans pay here.

source: Levin, van Kempen, Berger, Freund (2025) ChatDBG: Augmenting Debugging with LLMs
finding: A why-first LLM debugger with a debugger tool set was tested on Python bugs. Even the bare query 'why?' worked often, and a targeted question or a follow-up dialog helped.
numbers: 10 runs per program, gpt-4-1106-preview. Success: 57% with only 'why?'; 67% with targeted question; 85% with one follow-up. The follow-up gave no feedback on the first answer.
limits: Student-written programs, small scripts and notebooks; success judged by fix criteria set by the authors; one model family; authors note prompts may overfit GPT-4.
agent_relevance: Cheap gain: the same agent improves when it is asked to continue its reasoning once. Targeted expected-behaviour wording adds about 10 points.

source: Levin et al. (2025) ChatDBG
finding: Ablation of ChatDBG features: letting the LLM run debugger commands helped most when combined with richer stack traces. The backward-slice command was critical in notebooks.
numbers: LLM issued 0-12 commands per run, mostly info, slice, print. 'Without it, success rates rarely improved when the LLM took the wheel' for notebooks.
quote: Without it, success rates rarely improved when the LLM took the wheel.
limits: Ablation is per-program plots, no significance test given in the text. Slice used only for notebooks (ipyflow).
agent_relevance: Direct LLM evidence that backward slicing (Weiser style) is the load-bearing tool when state spans many cells or steps. Supports O5 plus a slice tool.

source: Levin et al. (2025) ChatDBG
finding: On C/C++ memory bugs ChatDBG explained nearly all crashes, but fixed the real root cause far less often than the proximate cause.
numbers: 36% of suggestions fixed the root cause; another 55% fixed the proximate cause. Each program run 10 times.
limits: Few real programs; fix criteria hand-set (Table 5).
agent_relevance: Backward reasoning reaches the symptom's neighbour more easily than the origin. Add a check: is this the origin of the bad value or only where it crashed?

source: Kang, An, Yoo (2024) Quantitative and qualitative evaluation of LLM-based explainable fault localization (AutoFL)
finding: AutoFL lets the LLM navigate a repo with function calls and explains the bug. It beat spectrum-based FL on acc@1 in Java and Python.
numbers: 798 real bugs. Method-level acc@1 up by 19.7% over Ochiai on Defects4J (GPT-3.5), 166.7% on BugsInPy (GPT-3.5), 233.3% on BugsInPy (GPT-4).
limits: Relative gains on small base numbers; public benchmarks may be in training data (a general contamination risk).
agent_relevance: LLM navigation tools work, but the gain is relative to weak spectrum baselines, not to human slicing.

source: Kang et al. (2024) AutoFL
finding: Explanations were often wrong or bland. Only one in five was an accurate cause description.
numbers: 300 sampled explanations: 20% accurate, 26.3% had at least one inaccurate statement, 46.7% bland. 83.7% of runs gave an explanation. At least one accurate explanation for 56.7% of bugs. Test score correlated positively with explanation quality.
limits: Manual labelling by the authors.
agent_relevance: Wrong why-stories are common. Need a verify step against runtime evidence before accepting a cause.

source: Kang et al. (2024) AutoFL
finding: Developers interviewed about explanations: most wanted them, with conditions.
numbers: 16 developers. 13 agreed or conditionally agreed FL would help; 12 wanted explanations (4 necessary, 8 useful). Value higher on unfamiliar code or hard bugs; 4 thought them unneeded for easy code.
limits: Interview study on pandas bugs; self-reported attitudes, not task performance.
agent_relevance: Moderator: unfamiliarity. The why-style aid matters most on code the agent has not seen.

source: Zhong, Wang, Shang (2024) Debug like a Human: LDB
finding: LDB gives the LLM block-by-block runtime values and asks it to verify each basic block. It beat text-only self-debugging.
numbers: HumanEval, GPT-3.5 seeds: baseline 73.8; Self-Debugging (SD) 81.1 (+7.3); LDB 82.9 (+9.1). Reported up to +9.8% across HumanEval, MBPP, TransCoder. Reflexion seeds 91.5 -> LDB(GPT-3.5) 95.1, LDB(GPT-4) 96.9, LDB(GPT-4o) 98.2.
limits: Short benchmark functions, visible test cases, same model debugging itself; gains on top of strong seeds are a few points near a ceiling.
agent_relevance: Runtime values at each step beat guessing from code. SD stalled after 2-3 iterations while LDB kept improving.

source: Zhong et al. (2024) LDB
finding: Self-Debugging with explanation or trace could fail to help: with a weak model it did not improve seed programs.
numbers: SD (+Expl.) and SD (+Trace) failed to improve seeds on HumanEval with StarCoder; authors say wrong model-made explanations misguide repair.
limits: Single benchmark/model combination.
agent_relevance: A model's own story about the trace can be wrong. Prefer real execution values over simulated ones.

source: Olausson et al. (2024) Is self-repair a silver bullet for code generation?
finding: Self-repair gains are small once compute cost is counted. The weak step is the model's feedback on why code is wrong.
numbers: Replacing GPT-4's own feedback with human feedback: overall repair success 33.30% -> 52.60% (1.58x); introductory 42.64 -> 62.21; interview 19.33 -> 45.67; competition 3.67 -> 14.67. 16 participants wrote 2 feedbacks each for 40 failing programs; 25 repairs sampled per pair.
limits: Human study N=16, 40 programs, online survey, no timing recorded. Self-contained Python tasks with unit tests. Strong-model feedback also helped weaker-model repair.
agent_relevance: Bottleneck is diagnosis (why did this fail), not repair. Spend scaffold effort on the cause-finding step.

source: Olausson et al. (2024) Is self-repair a silver bullet?
finding: Self-repair is not reliably better than just sampling more programs at equal budget, especially for small budgets.
numbers: Normalised pass-rate tables on APPS and HumanEval show many cells at or below 1.0 (for example 0.92 to 1.06 at 5 initial samples in some settings).
limits: Specific to the models and budgets of 2023-24; newer models may differ.
agent_relevance: Compare any added debugging step against plain resampling at matched cost, or the gain may be illusory.

source: Shahandashti et al. (2024) Program slicing in the era of LLMs
finding: Direct test of whether LLMs can compute static program slices on Java. They mostly cannot do it exactly.
numbers: 100 Java LeetCode programs. Static slicing Acc-D (partial match), GPT-4o: 30.91% zero-shot, 54.09% one-shot, 60.84% one-shot CoT; exact match max 7.33%. GPT-3.5 46.43%, Gemma-7B 43.43%, Llama-2-7B 17.57%. Neural baseline NS-Slicer 60.52% (CodeBERT), 0% exact.
limits: Short LeetCode programs, small open models; temperature 0.7-0.8; Acc-D counts partial overlap.
agent_relevance: Do not trust the LLM to slice by thought alone. Give it a real slicer or have it check each slice line against execution.

source: Shahandashti et al. (2024) Program slicing in the era of LLMs
finding: Dynamic slicing did not benefit from examples or CoT; GPT-4o was best zero-shot there.
numbers: Dynamic slicing GPT-4o: 59.69% zero-shot, 41.77% one-shot, 58.62% one-shot CoT; exact match 0% in all. GPT-3.5: 44.84 / 42.44 / 36.16. Best Llama-2 36.72%. Failure taxonomy: complex control flow most frequent root cause (39 cases); variable declarations and assignments the most common location. Prompt crafting +4%, iterative prompting +3.9%.
limits: Prompt tweaks gave only a few points; authors say prompt effects on the dynamic task were inconsistent.
agent_relevance: Another sign that a verified tool beats prompting for slicing. Prompt repair gives only about 4 points.

source: Guo et al. (2026) SWE-Doctor: runtime diagnosis from multi-faceted bug reproduction tests
finding: Running bug-reproducing tests and building runtime diagnoses (suspected fault location, symptom, reasoning) before patching raised resolution on SWE-bench.
numbers: Average resolved: SWE-bench Verified 75.7% (+2.0 vs mini-SWE-agent, +3.9 vs live-SWE-agent); SWE-bench Pro 59.4% vs 50.5% and 51.4% (+8.9, +8.0), five LLM backends. Ablation on 50 Pro issues (GPT-5.4-mini): removing runtime diagnosis cost 8.0 points; replacing multi-faceted tests with existing generators cost 8-10 points.
limits: Runtime-grounded diagnosis, not slicing as such. Ablation uses only 50 issues. Run-to-run SD 2.0 points over 5 runs on 50 issues.
agent_relevance: Evidence that evidence-from-execution before editing pays off on real repos, mostly on hard tasks.

source: Guo et al. (2026) SWE-Doctor
finding: Failed assumption: handing agents bug-reproduction tests as the target did not help patching.
numbers: Preliminary study with 3 advanced BRT generators in mini-SWE-agent: e-Otter++ variant resolved one fewer issue than baseline; AssertFlip made fail-to-pass tests for 70% of issues but resolved only two more. Fail-to-fail tests mislead agents.
limits: Preliminary study, one base agent.
agent_relevance: A reproduction test covers only one symptom; chasing a single symptom gives partial patches. Ask for all manifestations of the failure before going backward.

source: Liu et al. (2026) BluesFL: block-level instruction-oriented slicing for processor FL
finding: Slicing along instruction execution paths, plus signal values from waveforms, guided an LLM to localize hardware bugs far better than baselines.
numbers: 19K-line RISC-V core. Top-1: BluesFL 24 bugs (Top-5 28), Agentless 13, LiK 7, Tarsel-Tarantula 3, Cirfix 0, Strider 0. Ablation: w/o signal values 13 Top-1; w/o instruction path 5 Top-1. Cost $0.257 per bug; without signal values cost rose 609% (to $1.821) because it checked more blocks.
limits: One project, injected bugs, 7-page DAC paper; baselines run by the authors.
agent_relevance: Both parts of a human-style backward trace mattered: the path slice (which code ran) and values (what state). Slice cuts cost as well as errors.

source: Beck, Gehring, Kossen, Synnaeve (2026) Towards a Neural Debugger for Python
finding: Models trained to act as a debugger (step, breakpoint, forward and inverse execution) predicted program state well and transferred to code-reasoning tests.
numbers: 32B finetuned: forward next-state accuracy above 90% for step into/over/return/breakpoint; CruxEval input/output pass@1 66.5 / 83.2. 1.8B from scratch (150B tokens): 53.6 / 57.7. Inverse execution is ambiguous because execution is many-to-one.
limits: Predicts execution of small programs; not tested on real bug finding.
agent_relevance: Backward steps from a failure are many-to-one: the agent should keep several candidate causes, not one.

source: Weiser (1982) Programmers use slices when debugging, Commun. ACM 25(7)
finding: Founding study: programmers debugging were said to recognise code in the slice of the faulty variable more than other code. Not read this session; details from memory and unconfirmed.
numbers: Not verified. Figures unknown.
limits: Not opened. The ACM page returned 403. Treat every figure as unknown until read.
agent_relevance: Slicing as a mental strategy: people already work backward from the failing value. Needs a read of the original before citing numbers.

source: Parnin and Orso (2011) Are automated debugging techniques actually helping programmers?
finding: Often-cited user study on whether ranked fault-localisation lists help people; reported limited gains and that people did not follow the rankings faithfully. Not read this session; from memory.
numbers: Not verified. Figures unknown.
limits: Not opened; the Gatech PDF URL returned 404. Do not quote numbers.
agent_relevance: Warns that a tool that scores well on benchmarks may not change human (or agent) behaviour. Check whether the agent really uses the tool output.
